Case study, 001

COLAB

A sticky-note board that tells you who is doing what, without a spreadsheet.

RoleProduct & UI design
ToolsFigma, HTML/CSS prototype
FocusTeam visibility
StatusWorking prototype
01

Overview

The problem

Most small teams track who is doing what in a spreadsheet, a shared doc, or just memory. That works fine under about five people. Past that, it gets harder to tell who owns a task, or whether one lane of work is quietly overloaded while another sits empty.

The idea

A wall of sticky notes already solves this, informally, in a lot of studios and dev teams. COLAB keeps that feel: color, a little texture, a slight rotation per note, even a strip of tape. Then it adds two things a real wall cannot do: a lane that visibly fills up before it becomes a problem, and a click that isolates one person's or one team's work instantly.

02

The board

03

The small stuff

The physical details carry a lot of the design here. A strip of tape, a folded corner, and a few degrees of rotation per note are small touches, but they are the difference between a board that feels handled by a person and one that feels generated by a template. Getting that right took more iteration than the actual filtering logic did.

04

Key decisions

  • 01

    Color as the primary key

    Five roles, five colors, used consistently across the pills, the roster swatches, and the notes themselves. The same purple always means Design, everywhere on the screen, so nobody has to learn a legend.

  • 02

    Capacity bars instead of hard limits

    Rather than blocking a lane once it hits capacity, the bar just shifts color as it fills. It is information, not friction, so the board stays honest about workload without getting in anyone's way.

  • 03

    One interaction, two questions

    "What is this person doing" and "what is this team doing" reuse the exact same click-to-isolate interaction. One pattern to learn, instead of two separate filter systems.

05

Where it stands

This is a working front-end prototype, the same one shown in the screens above, built to test the interaction model before moving it into a proper Figma component library. Every filter, lane, and note in the live version is fully functional. Next up: drag-and-drop between lanes, and a real backing data model instead of a fixed board state.
